**Depreciation schedules for a $60 000 piece of equipment (estimated salvage = $10 000, useful life = 5 years)** | Year | Straight‑Line Dep. | Accumulated SL | Book Value SL | |------|--------------------|----------------|---------------| | 1 | **$10 000** | $10 000 | $50 000 | | 2 | **$10 000** | $20 000 | $40 000 | | 3 | **$10 000** | $30 000 | $30 000 | | 4 | **$10 000** | $40 000 | $20 000 | | 5 | **$10 000** | $50 000 | $10 000* | \*Book value equals the salvage estimate at the end of life. --- ### Double‑Declining Balance (DDB) – switch to straight‑line when it becomes advantageous The DDB rate is 2 × straight‑line = **40 %**. We apply DDB until the straight‑line expense for the remaining life would be higher than the DDB amount; at that point we switch to straight‑line (and we never depreciate below the salvage value). | Year | Beginning BV | Depreciation (DDB or SL) | Accumulated DDB | Ending BV | |------|--------------|--------------------------|-----------------|-----------| | 1 | $60 000 | **$24 000** (40 %) | $24 000 | $36 000 | | 2 | $36 000 | **$14 400** (40 %) | $38 400 | $21 600 | | 3 | $21 600 | **$8 640** (40 %) | $47 040 | $12 960 | | 4 | $12 960 | **$1 480** (straight‑line) | $48 520 | $11 480 | | 5 | $11 480 | **$1 480** (straight‑line) | $50 000 | $10 000* | \*Book value equals the salvage estimate at the end of life. --- ## What the schedules show | Method | Expense pattern | Why a company might choose it | |--------|-----------------|--------------------------------| | **Straight‑Line** | Equal, constant expense each year ($10 000). | • Matches a steady, predictable use of the asset.
• Simple to calculate and audit.
• Often preferred when the asset’s economic benefit is expected to be uniform over its life. | | **Double‑Declining Balance (with switch)** | High depreciation in early years (e.g., $24 000 first year) that tapers off, then levels out with straight‑line once it becomes “advantageous.” | • Provides an accelerated expense profile that can reduce taxable income earlier (tax‑deferred cash flow).
• Better matches the asset’s declining economic value or productivity (many assets are most productive when new).
• Allows a company to recognize more expense when the asset is most valuable, improving earnings management or matching cost with revenue. | ### Bottom line - **Straight‑line** gives a smooth, predictable expense that aligns with a constant pattern of use. - **DDB (switching to straight‑line)** front‑loads depreciation, giving higher early expenses and lower later ones—useful for tax planning or when the asset’s usefulness declines rapidly after installation. Both methods ultimately depreciate the same total amount ($50 000) over five years, leaving a book value equal to the estimated salvage of $10 000. The choice depends on the company’s financial‑reporting goals and tax strategy.
